statement.text: Given matrices $A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 3 & 4 \end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$, compute $AB$ and determine if $AB = BA$.

currentState.description: Before multiplying, verify the product is defined.

prompt.question: Can we multiply $AB$? What will be the dimension of the result?
prompt.hint: For $A_{m \times n} \cdot B_{n \times p}$, the result is $m \times p$.

correct.explanation: Correct! $A$ is $2 \times 2$ and $B$ is $2 \times 2$. The inner dimensions match (both 2), so we can multiply. The result will be $2 \times 2$.
correct.insight: Matrix multiplication is defined when the number of columns in the first matrix equals the number of rows in the second.

incorrect.1: The multiplication is defined because both matrices are $2 \times 2$ (inner dimensions match).
incorrect.2: The result dimension is (rows of A) × (columns of B) = $2 \times 2$, not $2 \times 4$.

currentState.description: Each entry is a dot product of a row from A with a column from B.

correct.insight: Each entry is the dot product of the corresponding row and column.

incorrect.1: Don't forget to add both products: $2(1) + 1(2) = 2 + 2 = 4$.

currentState.description: Apply the same dot product process for all entries.

prompt.question: What is $AB$?
prompt.hint: Compute each entry: $(AB)_{ij} = $ (row $i$ of A) · (column $j$ of B).

correct.insight: Systematic computation of each entry gives the full product matrix.

incorrect.1: Check your multiplication. For example, $(AB)_{12} = 2(0) + 1(3) = 3$, not 0.

currentState.description: Now compute $BA$ to see if $AB = BA$.

prompt.question: What is $BA$?
prompt.hint: Apply the same process: $(BA)_{ij} = $ (row $i$ of B) · (column $j$ of A).

correct.insight: Matrix multiplication is generally not commutative: order matters!

incorrect.1: If $BA = AB$, that would mean multiplication is commutative. Compute $BA$ carefully to see they're different.

keyInsights: Multiplication is defined when inner dimensions match: $A_{m \times n} \cdot B_{n \times p} = C_{m \times p}$
Matrix multiplication is NOT commutative: generally $AB \neq BA$
summary.fullSolution:
$A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 3 & 4 \end{pmatrix}$, $B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$

$AB = \begin{pmatrix} 2(1)+1(2) & 2(0)+1(3) \\ 3(1)+4(2) & 3(0)+4(3) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 3 \\ 11 & 12 \end{pmatrix}$

$BA = \begin{pmatrix} 1(2)+0(3) & 1(1)+0(4) \\ 2(2)+3(3) & 2(1)+3(4) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 13 & 14 \end{pmatrix}$

Therefore $AB \neq BA$. Matrix multiplication is not commutative.
